name: Apprenticeship and Knowledge Transmission Systems
summary: Structured person-to-person knowledge transfer — apprenticeship, mentorship, initiation, and pedagogical lineage — the mechanism by which every other keystone technology survives across generations.

claims.statement: Stone tool traditions (Acheulean, Levallois) show progressive refinement over tens of thousands of years that is impossible without structured teaching; experimental archaeology demonstrates these techniques cannot be acquired by observation alone

Medieval guild systems in Europe, Islamic waqf-funded madrasas, and West African griot lineages all independently formalised apprenticeship as the primary mechanism for preserving and transmitting complex knowledge

Indigenous knowledge systems (Aboriginal songline custodianship, Polynesian navigation apprenticeships, Andean quipu-keeper lineages) maintained precision scientific knowledge across centuries without writing, through structured mentorship and initiation

evidence.source: Stout (2011) Stone Toolmaking and the Evolution of Human Culture and Cognition, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 366(1567)
Epstein (1991) Wage Labor and Guilds in Medieval Europe, University of North Carolina Press
Hale (1998) Griots and Griottes: Masters of Words and Music, Indiana University Press
Kimmerer (2013) Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants, Milkweed Editions

notes: New social-domain entry. Teaching is the meta-technology: the one that transmits all others. Every entry in this codex — terra preta, quipu, damascus steel, the Great Law — survived because someone taught someone else. Modern economies discount mentorship because it is slow, relational, and unscalable. That is precisely why it works.
